title: Witchcraft Act of 1604: James I Hardens English Law
description: The Witchcraft Act of 1604, passed in the first year of James I's English reign, replaced the 1563 Elizabethan act with harsher provisions. The 1604 act extended the death penalty to a wider range of offenses, including consulting or feeding a familiar spirit (even without proven harm), invoking evil spirits, and digging up corpses for magical use — practices that required no demonstration of actual harm to a victim. This extension toward prosecuting intent and diabolical relationship rather than proved maleficium marked a theoretical shift in the direction of continental demonological assumptions. The act remained on the statute books until 1736 and was used in all subsequent English and colonial American witch prosecutions, including Salem.
historiographical_note: James Sharpe's Instruments of Darkness: Witchcraft in England 1550–1750 (1996) notes that despite the 1604 act's harsher provisions, English courts continued to require evidence of maleficium in practice — the gap between the law's theoretical scope and actual prosecution patterns is significant. The provision criminalizing familiar spirits without demonstrated harm is distinctly English; familiars are a feature of English witch belief rarely found in continental sources.
source_method: 1 James I c.12 (1604); secondary scholarship on English witchcraft legislation and James I's reign
